claims.text: The onset and progression of the phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements, notably Cu.
Cu surface segregation reduces the local melting temperature at nanoparticle surfaces.
Premelting initiates at the nanoparticle surface and propagates inward, producing spatially inhomogeneous melting.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are fully solid and have a uniform elemental distribution.
Particles should be heated under inert gas at a constant ramp rate, exemplified by 10 °C/min.
Comparing smaller and larger particles provides a controlled test of the effect of surface-to-volume ratio on segregation and melting.
A Cu-enriched surface layer forms through surface segregation and acts as a nucleation site for premelting.
At elevated temperatures, thermodynamic driving forces cause Cu to migrate to the nanoparticle surface.
Cu enrichment lowers the local effective melting point.
Localized liquid-like regions coalesce and broaden as the phase transition progresses.
Surface melting will occur before bulk melting and will be detectable as liquid-like boundary layers by in situ TEM.
DSC will show a lower-temperature endothermic event relative to the uniform solid baseline.
Smaller particles with higher surface-to-volume ratios will show more pronounced premelting and earlier melting than larger particles.
An inert atmosphere avoids oxidation effects during the proposed heating experiment.
Surface effects are significant for nanoparticles with diameters below approximately 100 nm.
The degree and temperature dependence of segregation may vary because of interactions among the alloying elements.
